title: Where Have All the Isms Gone?: On the Evolution of Knowledge
description: The roundtable examines how intellectual movements and paradigms have historically organized knowledge within disciplines -- from functionalism and structuralism in anthropology to postmodernism in various fields. The discussion explores whether contemporary scholarship has entered a phase where traditional movement categories no longer effectively structure academic thought. Key topics include Thomas Kuhn's paradigm shift theory, the Internet's fragmentation of knowledge dissemination, social polarization creating isolated communities of belief, and AI's generation of authentic and fabricated scholarly content. The organizers suggest we may be entering a new era in how knowledge is transmitted and organized across sciences and humanities.

title: Why We Write
description: The roundtable explores motivations behind writing through philosophical and literary lenses. The discussion examines how written words convey meaning, ranging from literal communication to deliberate ambiguity. Key themes include: the relationship between language and thought, writing's capacity to deceive or entertain, emotional purposes of writing, and William Empson's concept of ambiguity in literary expression. The panel considers what "animates writing" and creates texts that provide aesthetic pleasure.

title: Fail Again, Fail Better
description: The roundtable explores failure as a fundamental human experience, opening with Samuel Beckett's philosophy: "Ever tried. Ever failed. No matter. Try again. Fail again. Fail better." The discussion examines why people persevere after failure, using examples like NY Mets fans' loyalty despite repeated losses. Topics include Freud's concept of those "wrecked by success," practical wisdom from W.C. Fields, and whether failure itself can be rewarding or merely instrumental to future success.

title: See Memory
description: An afternoon exploring art, neuroscience, and storytelling featuring the New York premiere of the expanded 2025 edition of See Memory. This Bronze Telly Award-winning hand-painted documentary "brings the invisible workings of memory, trauma, and healing to life through over 40,000 individually painted frames." The film blends neuroscience with personal storytelling, followed by a multidisciplinary panel discussion.

speakerDetails.name: Viviane Silvera
speakerDetails.role: Artist & Filmmaker
speakerDetails.bio: Creator of See Memory "Telly Award-winning filmmaker and visual artist whose work bridges neuroscience, psychology, and fine art to explore how memory shapes -- and reshapes -- our sense of self."

speakerDetails.name: Daniela Schiller
speakerDetails.role: Professor, Neuroscience & Psychiatry, Icahn School of Medicine at Mt. Sinai
speakerDetails.bio: Research focus: "how the brain represents and modifies emotional memories" PhD from Tel Aviv University

speakerDetails.name: Cheryl Dolinger Brown
speakerDetails.role: Psychotherapist, LCSW
speakerDetails.bio: Nearly 50 years of clinical experience Specializations: trauma therapy, couples work Certified in Somatic Experiencing, Tapping Method, Imago Relationship Therapy

speakerDetails.name: Maura Spiegal
speakerDetails.role: Co-Director, Division of Narrative Medicine, Columbia University Irving Medical Center; Sr. Lecturer, Department of English & Comparative Literature
speakerDetails.bio: Teaching focus: fiction, film, family, memory, place, and affect

speakerDetails.name: R. John Williams
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor, English, Film and Media, Yale University
speakerDetails.bio: Author of The Buddha in the Machine: Art, Technology, and the Meeting of East and West Research areas: religion, futurology, systems theory, psychoanalysis, film and television

title: Resurgence of Freud
description: The event explores why Freud's theories experienced declining influence through the 20th century with advances in psychotropic medications and neurobiology, yet continues to resurface in contemporary practice. Key questions addressed include: "What is psychoanalysis's durable appeal all about?" and whether neo-Freudian concepts offer humanistic alternatives to AI-driven approaches. The roundtable examines psychoanalysis's resilience despite scientific critiques and its sustained role in humanities scholarship.

title: Neurodiversity
description: The roundtable explores how "neurodiversity recognizes variations in neurological function" while challenging deficit-based thinking. It examines empathetic approaches to supporting individuals with diverse cognitive experiences, questioning when assistance helps versus highlights personal struggles. title: Mindfulness Meditation: Benefits and Dilemmas
description: Mindfulness meditation is one of the most popular contemplative techniques in the world. Recently, however, a number of influential criticisms of the practice have emerged, many of which frame the technique as part of a larger neoliberal endeavor meant to privatize emotional well-being. Others have pointed to potential dangers of the practice, identifying cases where, for some people, it may actually trigger some of the dilemmas it is meant to treat, including anxiety, depression, and dissociation. And yet, it is difficult to find a major institution today that does not have some kind of training program or space devoted to various forms of meditation, accompanied by claims that it will help you live longer, enhance your performance at work, stay focused in an age of distraction, heal from trauma, and increase your compassion. What kind of reasonable expectations can one have regarding mindfulness? Has the practice become too commoditized to be effective? Is there an "authentic" mindfulness meditation? What philosophies of mind inform the practice? This roundtable will explore these and other questions on the way to gaining a better understanding of what the practice has come to mean today.

title: Music and Mind
description: The roundtable investigates "the profound connection between music and human experience," examining its mathematical foundations, neurological impact, cultural significance, and emotional resonance. The organizers note that music represents both rhythm and melody -- from ancient Pythagoras discovering celestial mechanics to contemporary neuroscience exploring how the human brain responds to musical patterns. The discussion touches on music's roles in creating community, triggering emotion, and reflecting cultural identity.

speakerDetails.role: Soprano Saxophonist/Composer
speakerDetails.bio: Pioneer in live electronics and movement in jazz Guggenheim Fellowship winner for music composition 45+ years developing unique soprano saxophone voice

speakerDetails.bio: Author of multiple works on music philosophy and aesthetic theory Scholar of musical history and philosophical inquiry

speakerDetails.bio: Elected to National Academy of Sciences and American Academy of Arts and Sciences Researcher on emotion, memory, consciousness, and brain interaction

title: Why War?
description:
This question is nearly always posed rhetorically, as in: there is no 'good' reason for war, is there? But responses to Why War? that grasp it literally are surely also called for. At the very least, merely insisting on war's moral vacuity has sadly failed to drive it to extinction. Writing two centuries ago Clausewitz claimed that 'war is the continuation of policy by other means'. This phrase concisely frames the problem this panel intends to address.

What really are the reasons for war? Definitionally, aggression is at its root. And yet aggression, both predatory and defensive, is a natural state, a form of behavior and a motivating force not limited to humanity. Does humankind express uniquely a surplus of destructiveness and sadism? If the answer to this question is yes, what then might account for this excess beyond Nature's provision?

A psychological response to this puzzle came in Freud's writings, but especially in Civilization and Its Discontents. Here Freud describes how social organization requires the repression of our inborn instincts, but the ensuing and unavoidable conflicts arising between individuals and groups simmer and ultimately boil over. Aggression then erupts in its destructive mode; push comes to shove comes to grenade, and so forth. Psychoanalysts following along Freud's path, among them Marcuse, Fromm, and Fanon, expanded his analysis into the sociological realm. According to these theorists it is a 'sickness' in the social structure – economic, racist, imperialist – that leads to greater frustrations and greater aggression; that social oppression and not simple psychological repression is what causes that excess of destruction beyond what we find in the animal world.

Our previous roundtable, Otherness, introduced another important element in this discussion. Xenophobia and nationalism seem to evolve and grow like weeds, both across the globe and as a constant strain within history. What role do nationalism and tribalism play in the indelible history of war? Most importantly, from among these reasons for war what might we address to bring an end to the sort of pain and suffering that is too horrid to contemplate without an injury to our souls?

title: Otherness
description: The roundtable examines the concept of Otherness through an interdisciplinary lens, exploring its origins, significance, and role in contemporary political polarization. Key questions addressed include: What constitutes Otherness? When did it emerge in Western thought? How did "Othering" become a verb? The discussion connects developmental psychology, phenomenology, and historical analysis -- particularly Hegelian Master-Slave dynamics -- to understand how we maintain recognition of others as subjects versus erasing them.

title: The Poetry of Aging
description: The roundtable explores how aging and mortality intersect with poetic expression. It addresses several key questions: "What is the relationship between dementia and language?" and "How does aging change the experience of reading and writing poetry?" Participants examine "the distinction between lived experience and the lyrical" and consider whether "poetry help us as we age." The event opens with historical literary references -- Shakespeare's meditation on aging ("Upon those boughs which shake against the cold") and Henry James's phrase "the distinguished thing."

speakerDetails.name: Rachel Hadas
speakerDetails.role: Professor of English, Rutgers University
speakerDetails.bio: Poet, essayist, and translator. Author of "Ghost Guest" (2023), "Pandemic Almanac" (2022), "Piece by Piece," and "Love and Dread" (2021). Forthcoming: "Forty-four Pastorals" and prosimetrum "From Which We Start Awake"

speakerDetails.name: Owen Lewis
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Psychiatry, Department of Medical Humanities and Ethics, Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Author of three poetry collections: "Field Light" (Distinguished Favorite, 2020 NYC Big Book Award), "Marriage Map," and "Sometimes Full of Daylight" (all Dos Madres Press). Three chapbooks including "Knock-knock" (2024). Awards: 2023 Guernsey International Poetry Competition, 2023 Arts & Letters/Rumi Prize, 2016 International Hippocrates Prize

speakerDetails.name: James Marcus
speakerDetails.role: Editor, Translator, and Critic
speakerDetails.bio: Author of "Glad to the Brink of Fear: A Portrait of Ralph Waldo Emerson" and "Amazonia: Five Years at the Epicenter of the Dot.Com Juggernaut." Translated seven books from Italian including Giacomo Casanova's "The Duel"

speakerDetails.name: Wendy Sloan
speakerDetails.role: Poet, Translator, Essayist; Retired Attorney
speakerDetails.bio: Former labor-side attorney (Hall & Sloan firm). Work published in "The Able Muse Translation Issue," "The Best of the Raintown Review," and "Poems for a Liminal Age"

speakerDetails.name: Caitlin Snow
speakerDetails.role: Geriatric Psychiatrist
speakerDetails.bio: Private practice in NYC. Medical degree from Weill Cornell Medicine; completed General Psychiatry Residency and Geriatric Psychiatry Fellowship at NYP/Weill Cornell. Former Assistant Professor of Clinical Psychiatry at NYPH-WCM

title: Come Out Wherever You Are: In Search of Consciousness
description: The roundtable explores philosophical positions on consciousness through three main perspectives. Panpsychism posits that "consciousness is a property of all matter, large and small, simple and complex." Eliminativism argues consciousness and phenomenal experience are illusory. The third approach, 4E Cognition (extended, embedded, embodied, enacted), proposes minds exist as "a dynamic amalgam of the world, our bodies, and our brains," extending beyond brain-centered models.

speakerDetails.name: Katalin Balog
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Philosophy, Rutgers University
speakerDetails.bio: Specializes in philosophy of mind, consciousness, and the mind-body problem

speakerDetails.name: Paul Boghossian
speakerDetails.role: Silver Professor of Philosophy, NYU; Director, Global Institute for Advanced Study
speakerDetails.bio: PhD Philosophy (Princeton), B.Sc. Physics (Trent University). Research focuses on epistemology and philosophy of mind

speakerDetails.name: Amy Cook
speakerDetails.role: Vice Provost of Academic Affairs & Professor of English, Stony Brook University
speakerDetails.bio: Published work on art, mourning, and 4E cognition; integrates cognitive science research into theatre scholarship

speakerDetails.name: John Hunter
speakerDetails.role: Professor & Director, Comparative & Digital Humanities Program, Bucknell University
speakerDetails.bio: Teaching focuses on digital networks, computing, robotics, and AI representation in media

speakerDetails.name: Barbara Montero
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Philosophy, University of Notre Dame
speakerDetails.bio: Research concerns physical substance and embodied movement (running, dancing, playing)

title: Synthetic Consciousness: Seeing and Believing
description: The roundtable explores the interconnection between vision and attention, examining how these faculties shape our perception of truth and falsehood. Core topics include animal consciousness, sensory perception, and cultural evolution. The discussion addresses how vision synthesizes other senses and provides evidence for claims of truth or falsehood -- connecting eyewitness testimony to certainty. The event also considers vision's role in creating images, written language development, and historical cultural evolution.

speakerDetails.name: Elissa Aminoff
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor of Psychology, Fordham University
speakerDetails.bio: Formerly research scientist at Carnegie Mellon University, Department of Psychology; adjunct faculty at Robotics Institute, Carnegie Mellon. Holds PhD in Psychology

speakerDetails.name: Kevin Chan
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor, Ophthalmology, Radiology, & Neuroscience, NYU Grossman School of Medicine; Assistant Professor, Biomedical Engineering, NYU Tandon School of Engineering
speakerDetails.bio: Completed doctoral studies in biomedical engineering at University of Hong Kong; recipient of Li Ka Shing Prize

speakerDetails.name: Paul Linton
speakerDetails.role: Presidential Scholar in Neuroscience and Society, Columbia University; Fellow of the Italian Academy, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Specializes in human 3D vision. Author of *The Perception and Cognition of Visual Space* (Palgrave Macmillan, 2017); lead editor of Royal Society volume *New Approaches to 3D Vision* (2023)

speakerDetails.name: Kenneth Miller
speakerDetails.role: Peter Taylor Professor of Neuroscience, Director of Center for Theoretical Biology, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Co-Director of Center for Theoretical Neuroscience and Neurobiology and Behavior Graduate Program. B.A. from Reed College; M.S. and Ph.D. from Stanford University; postdoctoral work at UCSF and Caltech

speakerDetails.name: Andrew Shum
speakerDetails.role: Entrepreneur, Software Engineer

title: Striking a Chord: Hearing and Space
description: The roundtable examined how vibration and sound shape human perception and emotion. Topics included the evolution from basic vibration sense to speech and echolocation, the role of the eardrum in spatial sound localization, and music's capacity to influence emotions. The discussion explored what's termed a "soundscape" as an emotional and value-laden space, incorporating rhythm, intensity, tone, and temporal dimensions that create depth and movement in auditory experience.

title: Discovering the What and the Wherefore: Scents and Sensibility
description: The roundtable examines olfaction as the first remote sense, exploring how smell creates "a series of pathways laid out on gradients" that orient organisms toward meaningful environmental stimuli. Key topics include how scent evokes memories, influences personal attraction and repulsion through body odor, and operates largely beneath conscious awareness while shaping cultural history and human motivation.

speakerDetails.name: Clare Batty
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor of Philosophy, University of Kentucky; Research Fellow, Centre for Olfactory Research & Applications, Institute of Philosophy, University of London
speakerDetails.bio: Specializes in philosophy of perception and olfaction

speakerDetails.name: James Bower
speakerDetails.role: CEO, Numedeon Inc.; Computational Neuroscientist; Visiting Professor, University of Hertfordshire; Affiliate Professor, Southern Oregon University
speakerDetails.bio: Computational neuroscientist

speakerDetails.name: Andreas Keller
speakerDetails.role: Neuroscientist & Philosopher
speakerDetails.bio: Holds PhDs in both neuroscience and philosophy; focuses on olfactory perception and psychophysics

speakerDetails.name: John McGann
speakerDetails.role: Director, Center for Cognitive Science, Rutgers University; Professor of Behavioral & Systems Neuroscience, Psychology Department
speakerDetails.bio: Directs the Center for Cognitive Science at Rutgers

speakerDetails.name: Dmitry Rinberg
speakerDetails.role: Professor, Department of Neuroscience & Physiology, NYU Grossman School of Medicine
speakerDetails.bio: Focuses on neural coding and olfactory processing

speakerDetails.name: Mark Smith
speakerDetails.role: Carolina Distinguished Professor of History, University of South Carolina; Claude Henry Neuffer Chair of Southern Studies; Fellow, Royal Historical Society
speakerDetails.bio: Historian of the senses

title: A =/= B -> Taste & Discernment
description: This roundtable explored how taste and discernment evolved from basic survival mechanisms to refined aesthetic judgment. The discussion examined the sensory biology of taste, the cultural history of culinary pleasure, and philosophical questions about whether taste is innate or acquired. Topics ranged from processed snacks to haute cuisine, exploring what drives preferences beyond financial means.

speakerDetails.name: Paul Breslin
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Nutritional Sciences, Rutgers University; Co-Director, Monell Science Apprenticeship Program
speakerDetails.bio: Research interests address sensation and perception, chemical senses

speakerDetails.name: Jerrold Levinson
speakerDetails.role: Distinguished University Professor of Philosophy Emeritus, University of Maryland; Past President, American Society for Aesthetics (2001-2003)
speakerDetails.bio: Author of five essay collections on music, art, and metaphysics

speakerDetails.name: John McQuaid
speakerDetails.role: Journalist & Author
speakerDetails.bio: Author of *Tasty: The Art and Science of What We Eat* (Scribner, 2015); won Pulitzer Prizes and numerous journalism awards

speakerDetails.name: Nils Noren
speakerDetails.role: Professional Chef; Director of Hospitality & Development, Chapman Ventures; Co-Founder & Director of Trade & Union
speakerDetails.bio: Former Executive Chef at KB restaurant (Michelin-starred); worked with Marcus Samuelsson at Restaurant Aquavit

speakerDetails.name: Danielle Reed
speakerDetails.role: Chief Science Officer, Monell Chemical Senses Center
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D. in Psychology from Yale; postdoctoral training in genetics at UPenn; studies individual differences in taste perception

title: Touch as the Ur-Sense: From Presence to Poesy
description: The roundtable examines touch as fundamental to sensation and sentience. It explores how sentience itself derives from feeling, and investigates the physical and neurological mechanisms behind tactile sensation. The discussion bridges scientific understanding with philosophical inquiry, examining how mechanical force creates neuro-electrochemical reactions at the skin's interface. Participants explore the transition from sensation to perception and consciousness, referencing Marcel Duchamp's concept of the "infra-thin" -- the boundary where sensation emerges -- and its poetic implications.

speakerDetails.name: Tapomayukh Bhattacharjee
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor, Department of Computer Science, Cornell University
speakerDetails.bio: Directs the EmPRISE Lab at Cornell. Ph.D. in Robotics from Georgia Tech. Previously NIH postdoctoral research associate at University of Washington

speakerDetails.name: Andrea Gadberry
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor, Comparative Literature, New York University
speakerDetails.bio: Author of "Cartesian Poetics: The Art of Thinking" (University of Chicago Press, 2020). Working on projects regarding early modern rationalism and literary causality

speakerDetails.name: Pascal Massie
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor of Philosophy, Miami University
speakerDetails.bio: Educated at Ecole Normale Superieure (France) and Vanderbilt University. Specializes in Ancient, Medieval, and contemporary continental philosophy. Author of "Contingency, Time and Possibility"

speakerDetails.name: Yalda Moayedi
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor, Pain Research Center, Department of Molecular Pathobiology, NYU College of Dentistry
speakerDetails.bio: Research on somatosensory neurons in the oral cavity and upper airway, investigating how sensory information guides oral functions including flavor perception

speakerDetails.name: Sushma Subramanian
speakerDetails.role: Science Writer & Journalist; Associate Professor of Journalism, University of Mary Washington
speakerDetails.bio: Author of "How to Feel: The Science and Meaning of Touch," exploring scientific, physical, emotional, and cultural dimensions of tactile sensation

title: The Effects of Media
description: What are the effects of media today? What exactly is 'social' about social media? How do media shape reality? Are developments in AI changing media as we understand communications technologies? Sixty years ago, the Canadian Professor of English and Media, Marshall McLuhan published the unexpectedly popular volume Understanding Media (1964), which would go on to establish a vocabulary addressing these questions — a vocabulary and set of ideas that scholars continue to grapple with to this day. But the world of media has shifted radically since then, and with the advent of social media and artificial intelligence the idea that 'the medium is the message' has taken on a kind of new urgency. This panel will address these questions, as well as those that deal with how we will define and experience media in the future.

title: Covid and Literature
description: This roundtable examined literature created during the COVID-19 pandemic. The event featured discussions of works including "Fractured: Covid 19 -- Memento Mori vs. Memento Vivere," "2020: One City, Seven People, and the Year Everything Changed," and "The Quarantine Tapes." Panelists explored how writers engaged with pandemic experiences through their work.

speakerDetails.name: Simon Critchley
speakerDetails.role: Hans Jonas Professor of Philosophy, New School for Social Research
speakerDetails.bio: Author of "Very Little...Almost Nothing" (1997), "Infinitely Demanding" (2007), "The Book of Dead Philosophers" (2009), "Tragedy, The Greeks and Us" (Pantheon, 2019)

speakerDetails.name: Richard Deming
speakerDetails.role: Poet & Critic; Director of Creative Writing, Yale University English Department
speakerDetails.bio: Award-winning poet and critic examining intersections of literature, philosophy, and visual culture; author of "This Exquisite Loneliness" (Viking, 2023)

speakerDetails.name: Eric Klinenberg
speakerDetails.role: Helen Gould Shepard Professor in the Social Sciences, NYU; Director, Institute for Public Knowledge
speakerDetails.bio: Author of "2020: One City, Seven People, and the Year Everything Changed," "Palaces for the People," co-author of #1 NYT bestseller "Modern Romance"

speakerDetails.name: Daphne Merkin
speakerDetails.role: Novelist & Critic
speakerDetails.bio: Known for candid commentary on family, religion, money, and sex; previously worked in book publishing

speakerDetails.name: Maria G. Pisano
speakerDetails.role: Book Artist, Printmaker, Curator & Educator
speakerDetails.bio: Publishes under Memory Press imprint; works in Library of Congress, 9-11 Memorial Museum, National Library of Medicine, major universities

title: Permanence and Impermanence of Mathematical Concepts
description: The roundtable examines how mathematical concepts have evolved throughout history. Starting with the concept of "five," it traces how humanity's understanding of numbers has transformed from concrete representations (five rocks) to abstract concepts. The discussion covers major revolutions in mathematics including non-Euclidean geometry and imaginary numbers, questioning how mathematics can claim to represent absolute truth when fundamental concepts undergo such radical changes.

speakerDetails.name: Michael Harris
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Mathematics, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D. from Harvard (1977) under Barry Mazur; previously at Brandeis and Universite Paris-Diderot; specializes in number theory; organized 20+ conferences

speakerDetails.name: Barry Mazur
speakerDetails.role: Gerhard Gade University Professor, Harvard University
speakerDetails.bio: Mathematician who teaches history of science and philosophy; authored "Imagining Numbers" and "Prime Numbers and the Riemann Hypothesis"

speakerDetails.name: Nathalie Sinclair
speakerDetails.role: Distinguished University Professor, Faculty of Education, Simon Fraser University
speakerDetails.bio: Co-editor of mathematics and aesthetics publications; developed TouchCounts and TouchTimes educational apps

speakerDetails.name: Alma Steingart
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor of History, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Researches mathematics and politics; works on democratic representation and mathematical reasoning in 20th-century America

speakerDetails.name: Jared Weinstein
speakerDetails.role: Professor, Mathematics & Statistics, Boston University
speakerDetails.bio: Number theory specialist; faculty member since 2011

title: Emotion
description: The roundtable explores fundamental questions about human emotion. "What is human life without emotion?" It examines how emotion has shaped human history and culture across millennia. Key topics include the relationship between neural signatures and emotional experience, whether emotions contribute to evolutionary fitness, the classification of emotions as a natural category, and possibilities for programming emotional responses into artificial intelligence systems.

speakerDetails.name: Mabel Berezin
speakerDetails.role: Distinguished Professor of Sociology, Cornell University; Director, Institute for European Studies, Einaudi Center for International Studies
speakerDetails.bio: Writes on challenges to democratic cohesion in Europe and the US; authored works on right-wing politics in Europe

speakerDetails.name: Katherine Elkins
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Humanities and Comparative Literature; Director of The Integrated Program in Humane Studies; Founding Co-Director KDH Lab, Kenyon College
speakerDetails.bio: Teaches philosophy-literature intersections and AI, language, and art; published "The Shapes of Stories" with Cambridge University Press

speakerDetails.name: Rob Hopkins
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Philosophy, New York University
speakerDetails.bio: Works in philosophy of mind and aesthetics; forthcoming book "The Profile of Imagining" (Oxford University Press) on sensory imagination; published on pictorial representation and picture perception

speakerDetails.name: Joseph LeDoux
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Neural Science, New York University
speakerDetails.bio: Research spans emotion, memory, consciousness, and their brain interactions; National Academy of Sciences and American Academy of Arts and Sciences member

speakerDetails.name: Rosalind Picard
speakerDetails.role: Founder & Director, Affective Computing Research Group, MIT Media Laboratory; Co-founder & Chief Scientist, Empatica; Co-founder, Affectiva
speakerDetails.bio: Over 350 peer-reviewed articles in AI and digital health; Empatica provides FDA-cleared biomarkers including seizure-detecting smartwatch

title: Shakespeare Forever
description:
The date of this Round Table is not a coincidence: William Shakespeare was born on or about April 23, 1564, and he died on April 23, 1616. This is a particularly auspicious year for celebrating Shakespeare: 2023 is the 400th anniversary of the publication of the First Folio, the first collected printing of Shakespeare's plays and one of the most important books in all of English literature.

Shakespeare's works remain as compelling as ever, and they are being envisioned in both traditional and often astonishingly new ways. In Boston, Chicago, Idaho, Kentucky, Lake Tahoe, Oregon, New York City and beyond, regional companies are gearing up for their annual sell-out summer Shakespeare festivals. The books and articles keep coming, and there is no end, it seems, to the new and different ways in which the Bard can be perceived: "All of Shakespeare's Plays Are About Race," declared a recent article in The Atlantic.

speakerDetails.bio: Writes celebrating queer communities and women's experiences; developmental theater leader

title: Life Beyond Earth: When and How Will it be Found?
description: Astrobiology examines potential life throughout the universe using Earth-based biological understanding. Since 1995, astronomers have identified over 5,300 exoplanets, with estimates suggesting more planets than stars exist universally. The galaxy contains approximately ten billion potentially habitable worlds. Life detection may occur within our solar system through challenging space missions or via exoplanet atmospheric analysis using the James Webb Space Telescope and ground-based observatories. Advanced civilizations might be identifiable through technological signatures.

speakerDetails.name: Chris Impey
speakerDetails.role: University Distinguished Professor, Astronomy, University of Arizona
speakerDetails.bio: Over 220 refereed publications on observational cosmology, galaxies, and quasars; $20 million in NASA/NSF grant support; eleven teaching awards; taught three online classes with 350,000+ students

speakerDetails.name: Lisa Kaltenegger
speakerDetails.role: Founding Director, Carl Sagan Institute to Search for Life in the Cosmos; Associate Professor, Astronomy, Cornell University
speakerDetails.bio: Pioneer and world-leading expert in modeling habitable worlds and their detectable spectral fingerprints; served on NSF committees

speakerDetails.name: David Kipping
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor, Astronomy; Director, Cool Worlds team, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Research in exoplanet demographics, detection techniques, exomoon search; published extensively in astrostatistics, astrobiology, technosignatures

speakerDetails.name: Rebecca Oppenheimer
speakerDetails.role: Curator & Professor, Department of Astrophysics, American Museum of Natural History
speakerDetails.bio: Comparative exoplanetary scientist; co-discoverer of Gliese 229B; studies direct observation and chemical composition analysis of exoplanets

speakerDetails.name: Sara Seager
speakerDetails.role: Astrophysicist; Professor of Physics, Planetary Science, Aeronautics & Astronautics, MIT
speakerDetails.bio: Holds Class of 1941 Professor Chair; pioneer in exoplanet research

title: The Techne of Memory
description: The roundtable explores fundamental questions about memory: "What is memory? How does it determine our experience and identity?" The panel examines memory as a process occurring both within and outside the brain, shaped by tools, infrastructures, social and personal experiences. Topics include how memory influences understanding of future and time, distinctions between individual and collective memory, and effects of externalizing memories through digital devices on identity and belonging. The discussion engages philosophical and neurological perspectives on mnemonic experience. Featured presentation: Viviane Silvera's film See Memory.

speakerDetails.name: Victoria Loustalot
speakerDetails.role: Author, editor, & communications consultant
speakerDetails.bio: 20 years in journalism, publishing, and digital media. Founding member and senior manager at Twitter, Conde Nast, and NBC. Teaching at Columbia, University of Arizona

speakerDetails.name: Sam McDougle
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor of Psychology, Yale University
speakerDetails.bio: BA in Neuroscience and Behavior (Vassar, 2009); PhD in Neuroscience and Psychology (Princeton, 2018). Postdoctoral fellow at UC Berkeley; joined Yale in 2020. Research in behavioral experiments, computational modeling, neuroimaging

speakerDetails.name: Daniela Schiller
speakerDetails.role: Professor, Neuroscience & Psychiatry, Icahn School of Medicine at Mt. Sinai
speakerDetails.bio: Professor in Nash Family Department of Neuroscience and Friedman Brain Institute. Research on how the brain represents and modifies emotional memories. PhD from Tel Aviv University

speakerDetails.name: Viviane Silvera
speakerDetails.role: Artist & filmmaker
speakerDetails.bio: Telly Award-winning filmmaker and visual artist bridging neuroscience, psychology, and fine art. Film *See Memory* uses 30,000+ hand-painted frames to explore memory's role in selfhood and healing

speakerDetails.name: R. John Williams
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor, English, Film and Media, Yale University
speakerDetails.bio: Author of *The Buddha in the Machine: Art, Technology, and the Meeting of East and West*. Published on religion, futurology, systems theory, psychoanalysis, and film/television

title: The Body and Psychosis
description: The roundtable explored how "4E Cognition" frames thought and behavior as "embodied, embedded, enactive & extended," drawing on philosophers like Merleau-Ponty and Heidegger. It examined how the body contributes to consciousness and how our social embeddedness shapes our sense of reality. Psychosis served as a test case for understanding disruptions to our shared world experience.

speakerDetails.name: Elias Dakwar
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor, Clinical Psychiatry, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Board-certified addiction and general psychiatrist researching novel addiction treatments with NIH support

speakerDetails.name: George Denfield, MD
speakerDetails.role: Neuroscience & Psychiatry Resident Physician, Columbia University & New York State Psychiatric Institute
speakerDetails.bio: Leon Levy Fellow in Neuroscience; BS from Tufts in biopsychology and cognitive science

speakerDetails.name: Vittorio Gallese
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Psychobiology, University of Parma; Director, Lab of Social Cognitive Neuroscience
speakerDetails.bio: Trained neurologist and fellow at Columbia's Italian Academy

speakerDetails.name: Siri Hustvedt
speakerDetails.role: Author and Essayist
speakerDetails.bio: Published seven novels and five essay collections exploring psychological and philosophical themes

speakerDetails.name: Gail Weiss
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Philosophy, George Washington University
speakerDetails.bio: Executive Co-Director of SPEP; authored monographs on embodiment and phenomenology

title: Living in Difficult Times
description: The roundtable addressed contemporary crises including pandemic impacts on life expectancy (particularly affecting Black and Hispanic Americans), increased homelessness, climate change, racist aggression, mass shootings, domestic political violence, and the Ukraine war. Organizers noted widespread societal division and psychological distress, citing commentary from journalists about global sadness and societal fear.

speakerDetails.name: Jon Chun
speakerDetails.role: Founding Co-Director KDH Lab, Kenyon College
speakerDetails.bio: Former CEO of privacy/anonymity website; Fortune 500 director; UC Berkeley entrepreneur; created first human-centered AI curriculum

speakerDetails.name: Katherine Elkins
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Humanities and Comparative Literature; Director, Integrated Program in Humane Studies; Founding Co-Director KDH Lab, Kenyon College
speakerDetails.bio: Teaches at intersection of philosophy, literature, AI, and language

speakerDetails.name: Farzad Mahootian
speakerDetails.role: Clinical Associate Professor, Global Liberal Studies, NYU
speakerDetails.bio: PhD Philosophy (Fordham); MS Chemistry (Georgetown); researches philosophy, science, mythology, and technology

speakerDetails.name: Edward Tenner
speakerDetails.role: Writer & Speaker
speakerDetails.bio: Independent writer covering science, design, culture; Smithsonian Lemelson Center founding advisor; Rutgers visiting scholar

speakerDetails.name: Steven Wein
speakerDetails.role: Supervising Child and Adolescent Analyst, New York Psychoanalytic Society and Institute
speakerDetails.bio: Member since 1993; Associate Dean for Child Analysis (2010-2016); Life Fellow, American Psychiatric Association

speakerDetails.name: R. John Williams
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor, English, Film & Media, Yale University
speakerDetails.bio: Author of "The Buddha in the Machine"; published on religion, futurology, systems theory, psychoanalysis, film/television

title: Coding and the New Human Phenotype: Is the Universe a Metaverse?
description: The panel explored the concept that "we have been living in a sort of metaverse all along." The discussion centered on the notion that the Universe functions as "one giant algorithmic computation" with information as the fundamental substance, and examined whether we might inhabit a simulation similar to The Matrix.

speakerDetails.name: Emily Adlam
speakerDetails.role: Postdoctoral Associate, Rotman Institute for Philosophy of Science, University of Western Ontario
speakerDetails.bio: Received PhD in relativistic quantum information from University of Cambridge; completed Perimeter Scholar's International programme in theoretical physics

speakerDetails.name: David Chalmers
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Philosophy and Neural Science, NYU; Co-Director, Center for Mind, Brain, & Consciousness
speakerDetails.bio: University Professor; authored *The Conscious Mind* (1996), *Constructing the World* (2010), and *Reality+: Virtual Worlds and the Problems of Philosophy* (2022)

speakerDetails.name: Elias Dakwar
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor, Clinical Psychiatry, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: MD, board-certified addiction and general psychiatrist; researched novel addiction treatments with NIH grant support for over a decade

speakerDetails.name: Christopher Fuchs
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Physics, College of Science & Mathematics, UMass Boston
speakerDetails.bio: Specializes in quantum information theory and quantum foundations; authored over 160 scholarly works; "Unconditional Quantum Teleportation" voted "Top-Ten Breakthrough of 1998" by Science editors

speakerDetails.name: Sylvester James Gates
speakerDetails.role: Clark Leadership Chair in Science, Distinguished University Professor & Regents Professor, University of Maryland
speakerDetails.bio: Theoretical physicist; John S. Toll Professor of Physics, College Park Professor Emeritus

title: Coding and the New Phenotype: In Search for Lost Time
description: The roundtable explores "how we discover codes, bearers of meaning, and how we reconstruct that meaning in archeology & paleoanthropology, in psychoanalysis, and in neuroscience research on memory."

speakerDetails.name: Gyorgy Buzsaki
speakerDetails.role: Biggs Professor of Neuroscience, NYU
speakerDetails.bio: Identified hierarchical organization of brain oscillations and proposed how these rhythms support "brain syntax," a physiological basis of cognitive operations. Changed understanding of information encoding in healthy and diseased brains, including epilepsy and psychiatric diseases. Known for the two-stage model. Bio link: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/gyorgy-buzsaki/

speakerDetails.name: Michael Novacek
speakerDetails.role: Curator & Professor of Paleontology, American Museum of Natural History
speakerDetails.bio: Senior Advisor to the Museum's President. Served as Senior Vice President and Provost of Science from 1994-2021. Doctoral degree from UC Berkeley; research focuses on paleontological patterns. Bio link: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/michael-novacek/

speakerDetails.name: Karen B. Stern
speakerDetails.role: Professor of History, Brooklyn College, CUNY
speakerDetails.bio: Interdisciplinary researcher with honors from Dartmouth College; M.A. and Ph.D. in Religious Studies from Brown University. Conducted excavations and field research across Mediterranean regions. Bio link: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/karen-b-stern/

speakerDetails.name: David Sulzer
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Psychiatry, Neurology, and Pharmacology, Columbia University & New York State Psychiatric Institute
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D. in biology from Columbia. Lab published over 250 studies on synaptic function, particularly basal ganglia and dopamine systems, plus neuroimmunology research. Bio link: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/david-sulzer/

speakerDetails.name: Marc Van De Mieroop
speakerDetails.role: Professor of History, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Historian of the ancient Near East and Egypt from writing's beginning through Alexander of Macedon's era. Previously taught at Oxford and Yale. Directs Columbia's Center for the Ancient Mediterranean. Bio link: https://www.helixcenter.org/participants/marc-van-de-mieroop/

title: Coding and the Human Phenotype: Manipulated Perception? Fakery, Authenticity, and the Birth of NFTs
description: The event explores "what counts as true and how we might know the truth in the age of coding." It addresses misinformation, knowledge decentralization, and challenges in establishing reality. The discussion examines how encoded algorithms provide security while risking privacy violations, and how technology enables creation of "convincing but misleading perceptions" and false narratives.

speakerDetails.name: Laura Edelson
speakerDetails.role: Postdoctoral Researcher, NYU
speakerDetails.bio: Co-directs the Cybersecurity for Democracy project with Damon McCoy, leading Ad Observatory and Ad Observer initiatives focused on digital advertising transparency, particularly during elections. Research examines misinformation spread patterns

speakerDetails.name: Andrew Guess
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor of Politics & Public Affairs, Princeton University
speakerDetails.bio: Combines experimental methods, datasets, and machine learning to study how people select, process, spread, and respond to information at the intersection of political communication and behavior

speakerDetails.name: Susana Martinez-Conde
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Ophthalmology, Neurology, and Physiology & Pharmacology, SUNY Downstate Health Sciences University
speakerDetails.bio: Award-winning neuroscientist and author; founder/Executive Director of the Best Illusion of the Year Contest; authored "Champions of Illusion" (Farrar, Strauss, and Giroux)

speakerDetails.name: Yotam Ophir
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor of Communication, University at Buffalo
speakerDetails.bio: PhD (2018, University of Pennsylvania). Uses computational text mining, network analysis, experiments, and surveys to study media effects in political, science, and health communication domains

title: Coding and the New Human Phenotype: Coding, Fiction, Metafiction -- the Parcellation of What Isn't There
description: The humanities examine idea manipulation. Ideas can be encoded, metabolized, and drive cultural evolution. The session explores roles cultural memes -- facts, factoids, or fiction -- play in this process and whether fiction offers insights into cultural dynamics.

speakerDetails.name: Peter A. Gloor
speakerDetails.role: Research Scientist, Center for Collective Intelligence, MIT Sloan School of Management
speakerDetails.bio: Leads a twenty-year Collaborative Innovation Networks project; Founder/Chief Creative Officer of galaxyadvisors; Honorary Professor at University of Cologne and Jilin University, Changchun, China

speakerDetails.name: Mark Hansen
speakerDetails.role: David & Helen Gurley Brown Professor of Journalism & Innovation, Columbia Journalism School; Director, Brown Institute of Media Innovation
speakerDetails.bio: 20+ years collaborating with designers, architects, artists; work exhibited at Museum of Modern Art, New York

speakerDetails.name: Yonina Hoffman
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor, English, US Merchant Marine Academy
speakerDetails.bio: Applies systems theory and phenomenology to 20th-century literature and systems novels; authored *The Voices of David Foster Wallace*

speakerDetails.name: Jonathan Kramnick
speakerDetails.role: Maynard Mack Professor of English, Yale University
speakerDetails.bio: Specializes in eighteenth-century literature, philosophical approaches to literature, cognitive science and arts; author of *Paper Minds: Literature and the Ecology of Consciousness* (2018)

speakerDetails.name: Nikos Salingaros
speakerDetails.role: Professor, Mathematics & Architecture, University of Texas at San Antonio
speakerDetails.bio: Architectural theorist and urbanist; authored *Algorithmic Sustainable Design*, *Anti-Architecture and Deconstruction*, *A Theory of Architecture*, and *Principles of Urban Structure*

title: Metaphysics
description: Physics examines Nature's fundamental properties; metaphysics investigates what must necessarily follow from those properties. For centuries, metaphysics provided the organizing framework for scientific research. However, 20th-century challenges emerged: quantum theory's Copenhagen interpretation emphasized epistemology over ontology, the "linguistic turn" discouraged claims beyond language's limits, and cognitive psychology shifted focus toward modes of cognition rather than Nature itself. Today, metaphysics experiences revival with refined understanding of empirical access to Nature. "Experimental metaphysics" now bridges quantum physics and metaphysical frameworks, while perceptual neuroscience analyzes ambiguous stimuli to inform consciousness studies. This roundtable examined how divergent perspectives -- sometimes paradoxical -- might be reconciled through metaphysics addressing these challenges.

speakerDetails.name: Harald Atmanspacher
speakerDetails.role: Physicist, The Collegium Helveticum (ETH Zurich, Switzerland)
speakerDetails.bio: Senior scientist and staff member at Collegium Helveticum since 2007. PhD in physics from Munich University (1986); previously research scientist at Max-Planck-Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics until 1998, then theory group head

speakerDetails.name: Elizabeth Barnes
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Philosophy, University of Virginia
speakerDetails.bio: Research spans metaphysics, social philosophy, feminist philosophy, and ethics. Author of "The Minority Body" on disability; currently writing on health's nature

speakerDetails.name: Hans Halvorson
speakerDetails.role: Stuart Professor of Philosophy, Princeton University
speakerDetails.bio: Extensive publications on quantum physics foundations, philosophy of science, and science-theology relationships in journals including Journal of Mathematical Physics, Physical Review, and British Journal for Philosophy of Science

speakerDetails.name: Gregg Jaeger
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Natural Sciences & Mathematics, Boston University
speakerDetails.bio: PhD Boston University; BSc in Mathematics, Physics, Philosophy from University of Wisconsin-Madison. Postdoctoral work in history of science (Dibner Institute, MIT) and experimental quantum-optical physics (NIST). Kavli Fellowship recipient

speakerDetails.name: Arkady Plotnitsky
speakerDetails.role: Distinguished Professor, Literature, Theory and Cultural Studies Program AND Philosophy and Literature Program, Purdue University
speakerDetails.bio: Published nine books and approximately 200 articles on continental philosophy, Romantic and modernist literature, mathematics and physics philosophy, and literature-philosophy relationships

title: Psychedelics
description: The roundtable explores how psychedelics -- substances that "manifest the mind" -- alter cognition, perception, emotion, and behavior. The discussion covers historical use in tribal ceremonies and warfare, the recreational popularity and subsequent restrictions of the 1960s-70s, and contemporary medical research. Current investigations examine psychedelics for treating mental illness, pain management, and end-of-life anxiety. The session notes that micro-dosing is being studied for PTSD, obsessive-compulsive disorder, body dysmorphic disorder, anorexia nervosa, and substance abuse treatment.

speakerDetails.name: Patricia Dailey
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor of English and Comparative Literature, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Co-Chair of Affect Studies University Seminar, Gender and Sexuality Studies Council, and Colloquium for Early Medieval Studies; author of *Promised Bodies: Time, Language, and Corporeality in Medieval Women's Mystical Texts*

speakerDetails.name: Elias Dakwar
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor, Clinical Psychiatry, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Board-certified addiction and general psychiatrist; researched novel addiction treatments with NIH grants for over a decade

speakerDetails.name: Nese Devenot
speakerDetails.role: Postdoctoral Associate, Institute for Research in Sensing (IRiS), University of Cincinnati; Affiliate Scholar, Center for Psychedelic Drug Research & Education, Ohio State University
speakerDetails.bio: Medicine, Society & Culture Research Fellow with Psymposia

speakerDetails.name: Alex Kwan
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor, Department of Psychiatry, Yale University
speakerDetails.bio: Neuroscientist studying antidepressant neurobiology using optical imaging to examine how ketamine and psilocybin modify brain circuitry; published in *Neuron*, *Nature Neuroscience*, and *Biological* journals

speakerDetails.name: Stephen Ross
speakerDetails.role: Research Associate Professor, Psychiatry and Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, NYU Grossman School of Medicine
speakerDetails.bio: Founding member of NYU Psychedelic Research Group; associate director of NYU Langone Health Center for Psychedelic Medicine

title: People & Things in Motion: Economics and the Future
description: The roundtable examined how economics intersects with contemporary crises. The organizers noted that "The Dismal Science seems to analyze and involve most aspects of our lives," expanding from traditional macroeconomics into behavioral economics and allied disciplines. The discussion focused on three critical challenges: climate change, mass refugee migration, and pandemic-related supply chain disruptions, analyzing their effects on inflation, unemployment, family structure, healthcare, education, and productivity.

speakerDetails.name: Nicholas Economides
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Economics, Stern School of Business, NYU
speakerDetails.bio: Internationally recognized authority on network economics, antitrust, and public policy; Founder and Executive Director of the NET Institute. Previous positions: Columbia University, Stanford University, UC Berkeley

speakerDetails.name: Robert H. Frank
speakerDetails.role: Henrietta Johnson Louis Professor of Management and Professor of Economics, Cornell University (Emeritus)
speakerDetails.bio: Writes "Economic View" column for The New York Times since 2005; B.S. in mathematics from Georgia Tech; taught math and science as Peace Corps volunteer

speakerDetails.name: Richard Howarth
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Environmental Studies, Dartmouth College; Editor-in-Chief, Ecological Economics
speakerDetails.bio: Environmental and ecological economist studying ecosystem services valuation, discounting theory, climate policy, and intergenerational justice

speakerDetails.name: Jennifer Jacquet
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor, Department of Environmental Studies, NYU; Director, XE: Experimental Humanities & Social Engagement
speakerDetails.bio: Deputy director of NYU's Center for Environmental and Animal Protection; research focuses on animals, environment, agnotology, and responsibility attribution

speakerDetails.name: David W. Schwartzman
speakerDetails.role: Professor Emeritus, Biology, Howard University
speakerDetails.bio: PhD in Geochemistry from Brown University; published "Life, Temperature and the Earth" (1999); author of "The Earth is Not for Sale" (2019)

title: Designer Genes
description: The roundtable explores how modern reproductive technologies have created unprecedented choices regarding offspring attributes. Historical context includes mythological and religious narratives about supernatural conception. Contemporary issues include sperm/egg/gene selection, polygenic screening of embryonic gene variants, and associated ethical considerations. The session examines "21st century options of sequencing and profiling once imagined as the realms of the gods."

speakerDetails.name: Nathaniel Comfort
speakerDetails.role: Professor, History of Medicine, Johns Hopkins University
speakerDetails.bio: Specializes in histories of genetics, eugenics, genomics, and biomedicine, plus bioethics. Author of "The Tangled Field: Barbara McClintock's Search for the Patterns of Genetic Control" (Harvard, 2001) and "The Science of Human Perfection"

speakerDetails.name: Henry Greely
speakerDetails.role: Deane F. and Kate Edelman Johnson Professor of Law, Stanford University; Director, Center for Law and the Biosciences
speakerDetails.bio: Specializes in ethical, legal, and social issues from biosciences. Founder and past President of relevant professional organizations

speakerDetails.name: Robert Klitzman
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Psychiatry, Columbia University; Director, Bioethics Program
speakerDetails.bio: Has authored over 150 scientific journal articles, nine books, and numerous chapters on critical bioethics issues

speakerDetails.name: Vardit Ravitsky
speakerDetails.role: Full Professor, Bioethics Program, School of Public Health, University of Montreal; President, International Association of Bioethics; Senior Lecturer, Harvard Medical School
speakerDetails.bio: Director of Ethics and Health at Center for Research on Ethics; 2020 Trudeau Foundation fellow

title: Stress
description: The roundtable explores stress as a universal human experience woven into language, thought, and emotion. It examines how stress manifests from various sources -- achievement, loss, change -- and its profound effects on brain development, cellular function, and aging. The discussion addresses both individual coping strategies and societal approaches to reducing stress through activism and justice initiatives.

speakerDetails.name: Allison Avery
speakerDetails.role: Vice President of Inclusion and Community, Dow Jones
speakerDetails.bio: Leads global diversity, equity and inclusion efforts with expertise in DE&I strategy, organizational culture, and learning development. Previously held senior DE&I roles at Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher and Flom, LLP and NYU

speakerDetails.name: Ben Bernstein
speakerDetails.role: Psychologist, Educator, & Author
speakerDetails.bio: Ph.D. in Applied Psychology from University of Toronto; Master's in Music Composition from Mills College. Fifty-year educator with expertise on performance and test stress. Bowdoin College honors graduate

speakerDetails.name: Charles Marmar
speakerDetails.role: Schub Professor and Chair, Department of Psychiatry, NYU Grossman School of Medicine; Director, NYU Center for Precision Medicine in Alcohol Use Disorder & PTSD; Executive Director, NYU Langone Military Family Center
speakerDetails.bio: Joined NYU in 2009; conducts clinical research on precision medicine approaches

speakerDetails.name: Ralph Wharton
speakerDetails.role: Professor, Psychiatry, Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons; Attending Psychiatrist, New York Presbyterian Medical Center
speakerDetails.bio: Research focused on psychotropic medications combined with psychotherapy or psychoanalysis; published research on lithium carbonate in affective psychoses

title: Panacea or Poison: Placebos and Nocebos in Modern Medicine
description: The roundtable explores how placebos "work" for medical conditions despite being inert substances. It examines the mind-body connection, asking: "what is the work they do?" The discussion covers how beliefs about medications can affect biology similarly to active drugs, the inverse nocebo effect (where negative expectations produce symptoms), and the mechanisms linking thought to physical health outcomes. Historical context traces placebo effects to shamanic practices, while raising ethical questions about modern clinical applications.

speakerDetails.name: Luana Colloca
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor, Pain & Translational Symptom Science, University of Maryland
speakerDetails.bio: MD, Master's in Bioethics, PhD in Neuroscience; post-doctoral training at Karolinska Institute (Stockholm) and NIH fellowship

speakerDetails.name: Kathryn Hall
speakerDetails.role: Director of Basic & Translational Research, Osher Center for Integrative Medicine; Assistant Professor of Medicine, Brigham and Women's Hospital & Harvard Medical School
speakerDetails.bio: PhD in Microbiology and Molecular Genetics from Harvard; 10+ years research experience

speakerDetails.name: Gerald Hurowitz
speakerDetails.role: Associate Director, The Helix Center; Assistant Professor of Clinical Psychiatry, Columbia University Medical Center
speakerDetails.bio: 30-year faculty member; full-time clinical psychopharmacology practice; founder and Chief Medical Officer of M3 Information

speakerDetails.name: Robert Klitzman
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Psychiatry; Director, Bioethics Program, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Author of 150+ journal articles and 9 books on bioethics; directs online and in-person Masters programs

title: Populism
description: Populism involves "political mobilization of 'the people' against a perceived elite caste of professional politicians." The roundtable explores what triggers such mass movements, examining whether Federalist Paper safeguards remain effective. Discussion covers perceived ruling-class failures, right vs. left-wing populism, and factors like nationalism, classism, religion, xenophobia, and domestic oppression. The page also examines whether anomie, alienation, social humiliation, and social media catalyze these movements globally.

speakerDetails.name: Jeffrey Alexander
speakerDetails.role: Lillian Chavenson Saden Professor of Sociology, Yale University; Co-Director of Yale's Center for Cultural Sociology; Co-Editor, American Journal of Cultural Sociology
speakerDetails.bio: Social theorist challenging anti-cultural reductionism in sociology

speakerDetails.name: Dhananjay Jagannathan
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor of Philosophy, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Teaches philosophy and classical studies; research focuses on Aristotle's ethics and political philosophy; completing manuscript on "Aristotle's Practical Epistemology"

speakerDetails.name: Takis Pappas
speakerDetails.role: Author & Researcher, University of Helsinki, Finland
speakerDetails.bio: PhD from Yale; comparative politics professor with positions at multiple universities (formerly University of Thessaloniki)

speakerDetails.name: Harry L. Watson
speakerDetails.role: Atlanta Distinguished Professor of Southern Culture, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
speakerDetails.bio: Native of Greensboro, NC; Brown University BA; Northwestern doctorate

title: The Many Minds of Memory
description: Memory functions as "a dynamic process, a stream of renditions and reflections" rather than static storage. The event explores how memory "conveys to us not what strictly happened, but embeds us in a retained internal moment." Key themes include implicit versus explicit memories, memory's paradoxical nature (private yet collective), and its role in identity and consciousness.

title: Ethics & AI
description: The roundtable explored how artificial intelligence challenges traditional notions of justice and anonymity. Drawing on John Rawls's "veil of ignorance" thought experiment, the discussion examined how AI's collection of personal data -- behavioral patterns, vocal characteristics, word frequencies -- creates detailed cyber-profiles that strip away anonymity. The conversation addressed how machine learning algorithms are deployed in medical, legal, mortgage, and sentencing contexts, often making predictions about individuals without their input. Key concerns included whether AI serves human interests and the ethical implications of algorithmic categorization affecting resource distribution and social opportunity.

title: How Deep Do We Go? Behavior, Mind, and The 4-Billion-Year History of Life
description: This roundtable examined Joseph LeDoux's book The Deep History of Ourselves: The Four-Billion-Year Story of How We Got Conscious Brains. The core premise challenges conventional understanding of human emotions as evolutionarily pre-formed states. LeDoux argues that single-cell microbes possessed basic survival mechanisms (detecting danger, seeking nutrients, maintaining fluid balance, reproduction) whose modern manifestations we interpret as fear, hunger, thirst, and pleasure. He contends emotions result from cognitive interpretation of significant life moments and require our specific brain architecture.

speakerDetails.name: Joseph LeDoux
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Neural Science, NYU
speakerDetails.bio: National Academy of Sciences member; American Academy of Arts and Sciences member. Research spans emotion, memory, consciousness and their brain interactions

speakerDetails.name: Kristen Lindquist
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor, Psychology & Neuroscience, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
speakerDetails.bio: Directs Carolina Affective Science Lab; uses behavioral science and neuroscience examining emotion

speakerDetails.name: Karl Joseph Niklas
speakerDetails.role: Liberty Hyde Bailey Professor of Plant Biology emeritus, Cornell University
speakerDetails.bio: Evolutionary biologist; over 400 peer-reviewed articles; research in plant biomechanics and evolution

speakerDetails.name: Gerald Hurowitz
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor of Clinical Psychiatry, Columbia University Medical Center
speakerDetails.bio: Associate Director, The Helix Center; 30-year faculty tenure; psychopharmacology specialist

speakerDetails.name: David Rosenthal
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Philosophy, CUNY Graduate Center
speakerDetails.bio: Coordinates Interdisciplinary Concentration in Cognitive Science; publishes on consciousness

title: Mathematics and Other Realities
description: The question of what the world in which we live consists of is as old as mankind itself. In philosophical jargon, this is the question of the ontological basis of reality. With the growing success of physics and other sciences, the idea of one fundamental ontology, that of particles and fields, became dominant as a physicalist version of ontology. However, as every hegemonial view creates alternatives, this one does too. This roundtable addresses two of them: (1) the Platonic idea that mathematics is prior to the tangible world of our experience, and (2) the idea of a tiered ontology, where each of its levels can achieve legitimate ontological significance. Both views reject the fundamental ontology of physicalist accounts, but they do so in different ways that will be discussed in this roundtable.

speakerDetails.name: Harald Atmanspacher
speakerDetails.role: Senior Scientist, Collegium Helveticum (ETH Zurich)
speakerDetails.bio: PhD Physics (Munich University, 1986); formerly at Max-Planck-Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics.

speakerDetails.name: Hartry Field
speakerDetails.role: Silver Professor & University Professor, New York University
speakerDetails.bio: Author of Science Without Numbers and Saving Truth From Paradox.

speakerDetails.name: Markus Gabriel
speakerDetails.role: Chair for Epistemology, Modern and Contemporary Philosophy, University of Bonn; Founder of New Realism
speakerDetails.bio: Germany's youngest philosophy professor (since 2009).

speakerDetails.name: Michael Harris
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Mathematics, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: PhD Harvard (1977); specializes in number theory.

speakerDetails.name: Kristopher McDaniel
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Philosophy, University of Notre Dame
speakerDetails.bio: PhD University of Massachusetts-Amherst (2004).

speakerDetails.name: Alma Steingart
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor of History, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Researches connections between mathematics and politics.

title: Emergence of Empathy: Encountering The Other Through Fiction
description: The event explores how empathy -- derived from Greek "pathos" meaning "to endure" -- functions through fiction. Coined in 1909 by psychologist Edward Bradford Titchner as a translation of German "Einfuhlung," empathy represents an emotional strategy to "feel into" others and resolve internal conflicts. The roundtable examines how fictional narratives shape our understanding of intimate human experiences including love, death, friendship, loss, and fear through imaginary characters we encounter in beloved books.

speakerDetails.name: Percival Everett
speakerDetails.role: Distinguished Professor of English, University of Southern California; Author
speakerDetails.bio: Prolific author of approximately thirty books, mostly novels. Recipient of the 2018 Distinguished Achievement Award from the Western Literature Association.

speakerDetails.name: Siri Hustvedt
speakerDetails.role: Author, Essayist
speakerDetails.bio: Author of poetry collection "Reading to You," seven novels including "The Blindfold" and "The Blazing World," and five essay collections addressing literature and human experience.

speakerDetails.name: Yiyun Li
speakerDetails.role: Author; Professor of Creative Writing, Princeton University
speakerDetails.bio: Author of six books including story collections and novels. Named MacArthur Foundation Fellow in 2010.

speakerDetails.name: Joseph Luzzi
speakerDetails.role: Asher B. Edelman Professor of Literature, Bard College; Author
speakerDetails.bio: PhD Yale. Author of nine books including recent works on Renaissance art and literature.

speakerDetails.name: Alberto Manguel
speakerDetails.role: Writer and Translator
speakerDetails.bio: Argentinian-Canadian writer and critic. Former director of Argentine National Library until August 2018. Recipient of Formentor Prize (2017) and Gutenberg Prize (2018).

title: Mechanization of Math
description: The roundtable explores how mathematical proofs too complex for human verification are now being certified by machine systems. It addresses whether mathematics should require computer-readable code and questions whether AI will replace human mathematicians. The discussion centers on whether mathematics is a practical tool or an intrinsically human endeavor with inherent value.

speakerDetails.name: Stephanie Dick
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor of History and Sociology of Science, University of Pennsylvania
speakerDetails.bio: PhD in History of Science from Harvard University in 2015; Junior Fellow at the Harvard Society of Fellows prior to joining Penn.

speakerDetails.name: Branden Fitelson
speakerDetails.role: Distinguished Professor of Philosophy, Northeastern University
speakerDetails.bio: Previously held teaching positions at Rutgers, UC-Berkeley, San Jose State, and Stanford.

speakerDetails.name: Thomas Callister Hales
speakerDetails.role: Mellon Professor of Mathematics, University of Pittsburgh
speakerDetails.bio: BS and MS degrees from Stanford University, Tripos Part III from Cambridge University, PhD from Princeton University in representation theory.

speakerDetails.name: Michael Harris
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Mathematics, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: PhD in 1977 from Harvard University, under the direction of Barry Mazur. Organized or co-organized more than 20 conferences.

speakerDetails.name: Francesca Rossi
speakerDetails.role: IBM Fellow & IBM AI Ethics Global Leader, IBM T.J. Watson Research Lab, New York
speakerDetails.bio: Co-chairs IBM AI Ethics board; participates in many global multi-stakeholder initiatives on AI ethics.

title: Lying
description: The roundtable explores the complexities of truth-telling beyond simple factual accuracy. It examines how omissions can create false impressions, the nature of lies versus truth statements, and psychological dimensions of pathological lying. Topics include confabulation, sociopathy, and case studies like Elizabeth Holmes/Theranos, exploring "what makes these tales so fascinating" as liars employ various deceptive tactics.

speakerDetails.name: Anna Balas
speakerDetails.role: Associate Professor, Clinical Psychiatry, Weill Cornell Medical College; Training & Supervising Analyst, New York Psychoanalytic Institute
speakerDetails.bio: 35+ years private practice in adult and child psychiatry; Distinguished Fellow, American Psychiatric Association.

speakerDetails.name: Neil Garrett
speakerDetails.role: Henry Wellcome Research Fellow in Cognitive Neuroscience, Oxford University
speakerDetails.bio: Research focuses on aversive behavior, learning, and emotional adaptation in decision-making.

speakerDetails.name: Emma Levine
speakerDetails.role: Assistant Professor of Behavioral Science, University of Chicago Booth School of Business; Charles Merrill Faculty Scholar
speakerDetails.bio: Rising Star, Association of Psychological Science (2019); studies psychology of altruism, trust, and ethics.

speakerDetails.name: Francis X. Shen
speakerDetails.role: Executive Director, Harvard MGH Center for Law, Brain, and Behavior; Instructor, Harvard Medical School; Senior Fellow, Harvard Law School Petrie-Flom Center; Associate Professor of Law, McKnight Presidential Fellow

speakerDetails.name: Jonathan Stray
speakerDetails.role: Research Scholar/Computational Journalist, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Teaches dual master's program; contributor to NY Times, Atlantic, Wired, Foreign Policy, ProPublica; former Interactive Technology Editor.

title: Status
description: A recent New York Times article proclaimed "status anxiety" one of the defining preoccupations of our time (Michelle Goldberg, "Status Anxiety and the Scam Economy," March 15, 2019). But what are we really anxious about? What, in fact, is status and why do we want it? This Helix discussion will consider that complex question from a variety of different perspectives—historical, psychological, sociological, and biological. Together we hope to generate insights about what it is that so many of us pursue and think we want.

speakerDetails.name: W. Warner Burke
speakerDetails.role: E.L. Thorndike Professor of Psychology and Education, Teachers College, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Teaches leadership and organizational change; researches learning agility and multi-rater feedback; authored/co-authored 21 books.

speakerDetails.name: James L. Fuller
speakerDetails.role: Research Fellow, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: PhD focused on vocal signal evolution in primates; began working with wild primates in Kenya in 1995.

speakerDetails.name: David Levine
speakerDetails.role: Professor of the Practice of Performance, Theater, and Media, Harvard University
speakerDetails.bio: Work spans theater, performance, video, photography; exhibited at Brooklyn Museum, MoMA, Creative Time.

speakerDetails.name: Darrin McMahon
speakerDetails.role: Mary Brinsmead Wheelock Professor of History, Dartmouth College
speakerDetails.bio: Educated at UC Berkeley and Yale; PhD 1998.

speakerDetails.name: Tayarisha Poe
speakerDetails.role: Independent Filmmaker
speakerDetails.bio: Selected as one of 25 New Faces by Filmmaker Magazine (2015); Sundance Institute Knight Foundation Fellow (2016).

title: Shame
description: The roundtable examined shame as a societal mechanism, addressing when and why shaming occurs, who profits from it, and how power dynamics operate through shame. Key questions included when shame is justified versus cruel, and how shame functions in the age of big data. The discussion covered shame's role in politics, social media platforms profiting from online interactions, and automated scoring systems affecting employment, education, and criminal sentencing.

speakerDetails.name: Joseph Adamson
speakerDetails.role: Professor Emeritus of English, McMaster University
speakerDetails.bio: Focus: Research on Silvan Tomkins' affect and script theory, shame dynamics in literature and writers' lives.

speakerDetails.name: Michael Lewis
speakerDetails.role: University Distinguished Professor of Pediatrics and Psychiatry, Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School
speakerDetails.bio: Director of Institute for Study of Child Development; Professor of Psychology, Education, Biomedical Engineering, and Social Work at Rutgers University; Executive Committee member of Child Development Center.

speakerDetails.name: Cathy O'Neil
speakerDetails.role: Ph.D. in Mathematics (Harvard), postdoc (MIT), former professor (Barnard College); previously worked as quantitative analyst for D.E. Shaw hedge fund.

speakerDetails.name: Richard A. Shweder
speakerDetails.role: Harold Higgins Swift Distinguished Service Professor of Human Development, University of Chicago
speakerDetails.bio: Cultural anthropologist; Ph.D. in social anthropology (Harvard, 1972).

title: Living in the Anthropocene
description: The roundtable explores conceptual questions about characterizing our planet's current era, examining distinctions between "human subjects and the non-human realm, between nature and artifice, between agency and objectivity." Panelists approach these topics through literary, philosophical, scientific, and psychological perspectives to consider how such reflection might enhance human agency during an ongoing crisis.

speakerDetails.name: Akeel Bilgrami
speakerDetails.role: Sidney Morgenbesser Professor of Philosophy, Columbia University

speakerDetails.name: Amitav Ghosh
speakerDetails.role: Author; wrote *The Great Derangement: Climate Change and the Unthinkable* (2016)

speakerDetails.name: Dale Jamieson
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Environmental Studies and Philosophy, NYU; authored *Reason in a Dark Time*

speakerDetails.name: John Kress
speakerDetails.role: Distinguished Scientist & Curator of Botany, Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History

speakerDetails.name: Donald Moss
speakerDetails.role: Program Chair of APsaA; founding member of Green Gang (analysts/scientists focused on climate change)

speakerDetails.name: Nermeen Shaikh
speakerDetails.role: Co-Host & News Producer, Democracy Now!

title: Life in the Universe
description: The roundtable explores "the notion of life in the universe and what it might look like elsewhere" given billions of observable stars and galaxies intriguing both scientists and philosophers.

speakerDetails.name: Ken Dill
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Physics and Chemistry, Stony Brook University; Director, Laufer Center for Physical Biology
speakerDetails.bio: Helped solve the protein folding problem; researches protein principles, cell evolution, and early molecular origins of life; authored two textbooks on physics.

speakerDetails.name: Priyamvada Natarajan
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Astronomy and Physics, Yale University
speakerDetails.bio: Focuses on dark matter, dark energy, and black holes; made key contributions mapping dark matter distribution and tracing black hole growth history using gravitational lensing.

speakerDetails.name: Dennis Overbye
speakerDetails.role: Cosmic Affairs Correspondent, New York Times
speakerDetails.bio: Covers topics from black hole behavior to science in media; authored "Lonely Hearts of the Cosmos."

speakerDetails.name: Caleb Scharf
speakerDetails.role: Director of Astrobiology, Columbia University
speakerDetails.bio: Spans cosmology, exoplanetary science, and astrobiology; Global Science Coordinator for Earth-Life Science Institute's Origins Network.

speakerDetails.name: Edwin Turner
speakerDetails.role: Professor of Astrophysical Sciences, Princeton University; Affiliate Scientist, University of Tokyo's Kavli Institute
speakerDetails.bio: SB Physics (MIT '71), PhD Astronomy (Caltech '75).
